summary: Defines a new option for IPv6 Router Advertisement messages that provides more flag bits. The original flags field was close to running out of space as protocols reserved bits. It was replaced by RFC 5175.

eli5.summary: The little box of yes-or-no switches in router announcements was filling up. This adds a bigger box. It was replaced by RFC 5175.

questions: how to extend ipv6 router advertisement flags
subtitle: Extend the space for control flags in IPv6 router announcements.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Router Advertisement messages have only 8 bits reserved for flags that control various behaviors. As protocols reserved more of these bits for new features, the field was approaching exhaustion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5075 defines a new Neighbor Discovery option that provides 48 additional flag bits within Router Advertisement messages, allowing far more protocols to reserve their own bits.
tldr.outcome: The Router Advertisement protocol can now support new features without creating a tight bottleneck on flag bits. RFC 5175 later replaced this with a slightly different approach.

today: RFC 5075 was obsoleted by RFC 5175, which provides a revised approach to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery parameter assignment. However, the fundamental concept of extending flag space through options remains important to IPv6's flexibility.

sections.title: The Flag Space Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 networks use a protocol called Neighbor Discovery (NDP) to let routers announce their presence and capabilities to hosts. These announcements, called Router Advertisements (RA), contain an 8-bit field with single-bit flags that control important behaviors: whether addresses are managed by the network (M flag), whether other configuration is available (O flag), whether the router is a Mobile IPv6 home agent (H flag), and several others.

Multiple Internet protocols have reserved bits in this 8-bit field for their own purposes. With various protocols in development that also needed flag bits, it became clear that the original 8 bits would not be sufficient. RFC 5075 solves this by defining a new optional field in the Router Advertisement message that provides 48 additional flag bits.
sections.eli5: Router announcements use 8 yes-or-no switches to control how IPv6 networks work. Different protocols wanted to use more and more of these switches. This document adds 48 more switches.

sections.title: The Expanded Flags Option
sections.content:
The new field, called the RA Flags Extension Option (EFO) or Expanded Flags Option, is defined as a standard Neighbor Discovery option that can be included in Router Advertisement messages. It has a type field (assigned as type 26), a length field, and 48 bits available for assignment by protocols that need them.

The option follows several strict rules: it must appear only in Router Advertisement messages (never elsewhere), it must appear before any other options that depend on its flags, there can only be one instance per RA message, and all unused flag bits must be set to zero. A receiver that sees this option must ignore unknown flag bits and handle different message lengths gracefully to allow for future expansion.
sections.eli5: The new option is just a list of 48 extra switches that can be included in router announcements. If a receiver does not understand a switch, it should just ignore it.

sections.title: Flag Numbering and Usage
sections.content:
The flag bits in the RA Flags Extension Option are numbered from 8 to 55, continuing the numbering of the original 8 RA flags (bits 0 to 7, which remain in the main RA message header). The bits are numbered from left to right in the option, and the specific allocation of these bits is determined by protocols that request them through the IANA standards process.

Some bits are reserved for future use, and bits 54 and 55 are designated for private experimentation. When a protocol defines a new flag, it must reserve a specific bit number and describe the meaning and usage of that flag in its RFC.
sections.eli5: The new switches are numbered 8 through 55, continuing from the original 8 switches. Different protocols can claim different switches for their own purposes.

sections.title: When to Include the Option
sections.content:
The option has clear construction and reception requirements. When building a Router Advertisement message, the sender must include this option only if at least one flag bit within it is set to one (if all bits are zero, the option is omitted). The option must appear early in the message, before any other options that depend on the flags it carries, to allow receivers to understand the context of those subsequent options.

Receivers must follow specific rules: ignore the option if it appears anywhere except in a Router Advertisement message, ignore any copies after the first one, check that the length field is at least 1, and safely skip over any unknown flag bits or future extensions by checking the length field.
sections.eli5: You only send the new switches if you are actually using at least one of them. And the receiver should ignore switches it does not recognize.

fields.desc: Option type; 26 for RA Flags Extension

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of option in 8-octet units; must be at least 1

fields.name: Flag bits
fields.desc: 48 bits available for assignment; bits 8-55 continuing from RA header
